category_title: Students who procrastinate on work plans until the final deadline
minimal_context: The student is sitting in a study lesson with a new multi-week work plan for math and science.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Here is the new math and science work plan for the next three weeks. You can go ahead and start working at your own pace.

STUDENT: (Puts the work plan on the desk and stares at it without opening the book) Okay.

TUTOR: What do you think you will work on first?

STUDENT: I don't know. I normally procrastinate because I struggle to get started.

TUTOR: Well, just try your best to get something done during this study lesson.

STUDENT: (Leans back in the chair) This is how I normally work: At school, the first couple of weeks, I do nothing. I'll just delay the work plan until the last few days.

options.A: Agree with the student that they are having a rough time getting started on the work plan.
options.B: Deliver verbal statements or gestures (e.g., high five, thumbs up) indicating approval beyond simple acknowledgment.
options.C: Ignore the student's procrastination and refusal to start the work plan (where safe to do so).
options.D: Break the work plan into clear learning objectives, short-term tasks, and tightly scheduled activities with clear targets.
